newsitem.title: USA: Citicorp sees card losses stabilizing.
newsitem.headline: Citicorp sees card losses stabilizing.

text.p: Citicorp executive vice president and principal financial officer Thomas Jones told analysts in a telephone conference call there are signs credit losses in its U.S. charge card business are stabilizing.
Jones also said a share buyback program, which is nearing the maximum authorized by the company's board of directors, will continue.

"We see signs of stabilization on the card side," Jones told the analysts. Earlier Tuesday, in the third quarter earnings release, Citicorp said the loss ratio in U.S. cards was 5.11 percent for the third quarter of 1966, compared to 4.99 percent in the second quarter.
"We see some signs of stabilizing on the card side," Jones said.
Asked later in a session with reporters if the company is cutting back on card solicitations to consumers, Jones said the company is keeping a "fairly low profile."

On the question of share buybacks, Jones said, "we've said now for two years or so that we will use excess capital over and above that which we need to fund good businesses, growing businesses, to buy back stock." He repeated "the program will continue."

Asked if share buybacks made sense in view of the share price hitting a new high in the mid-90's Tuesday, Jones said the market multiple on the stock is only 63 percent of the multiple on the Standard & Poor's 500 index, so buying in stock still looks like a good value. In the third quarter, Citicorp repurchased 8.9 million shares of common.

Asked about a shortfall in the ratio of incremental revenue to expense to 1.7 to 1.0 in the quarter, which compared to a corporate goal of 2.0 to 1.0, Jones said the company never committed to achieving 2.0 or higher in each and every quarter. He said expenses are uneven from one quarter to the next. "In the emerging markets we had unusually high expense growth this quarter," he said. He also said the ratio is 2.1 to 1 for the first nine months of the year and added that 2.0 to 1.0 for the full year can be achieved.
The 1.7 calculation excludes a $40 million after-tax charge related to the U.S. Savings Association Insurance Fund (SAIF).
